Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Replication fork reversal is a protective mechanism during DNA replication stress that occurs when replication forks encounter an obstacle and reverse their course, forming a four-way "chicken foot" structure through the annealing of newly synthesized DNA strands, while the parental strands re-anneal. This structure has gained significant interest over the past decade, as it stabilizes the replication fork, prevents DNA damage, and allows time for repair. As stated by the authors, direct analysis of these structures requires complex electron microscopy-based techniques, mastered by only a few specialized laboratories worldwide. In this article, Roy and colleagues propose an elegant new approach to monitor fork reversal using a modified proximity ligation assay (PLA) that specifically detects EdU on the regressed arm of the reversed fork. The assay is based on the bold assumption that EdU epitopes incorporated into the two sister chromatids of a normal Y-shaped fork do not generate a PLA signal, due to their physical separation—even though they are held together by cohesin. Nevertheless, the authors convincingly demonstrate a specific RF-SIRF signal at reversed forks, normalized to total EdU incorporation. They further show that this signal increases upon treatment with drugs known to induce fork reversal and is lost following depletion of SMARCAL1, a key factor involved in fork reversal. Additionally, they show that this assay provides insights into the subnuclear organization of reversed forks, the presence of single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) at reversed forks, and their relative frequency during S phase. Altogether, RF-SIRF emerges as a promising assay that complements indirect methods such as DNA fiber analysis and serves as an accessible alternative to electron microscopy. This approach fulfills a clear need in the field and will be of great utility to the growing number of laboratories investigating replication stress responses and fork reversal. However, the authors should address the following points to strengthen their conclusions:
1. Simultaneous click chemistry using biotin-azide and Alexa488-azide may compete for the single alkyne group on EdU. This competition could significantly impact data interpretation and may explain the substantial variability observed in EdU-PLA signals across biological replicates, as shown in Extended Data Fig. 1.
Variability in PLA experiments is a well-known phenomenon and intrinsic to PLA technology (see eg. PMC8041061), but not specific to RF SIRF or to EdU reactions.
Yes, Alexa488 and biotin azides do compete for EdU moieties, which is by design. The azides are applied at the same time, so are in steady state equilibrium and have the same relative chances for chemical addition within a given experiment (e.g. same chance between the conditions tested). Given that Click-it is a chemical reaction, there seems to be no logical reason to believe it could explain variability in EdU-PLA signals.
2. In the legend of Extended Data Fig. 1a, the authors mention anti-biotin primary antibodies. These should presumably be derived from two different species (e.g., mouse and rabbit). The authors should clarify this in the Methods section.
Yes, we utilize two anti-biotin antibodies from two different species. We now better clarify this in the methods section.
3. In the ssDNA-SIRF assay, what is the minimum ssDNA length required for effective recognition by the anti-ssDNA antibody?
The antibody is raised against denatured calf thymus, so the minimum ssDNA length is not defined. We are not able to make a ssDNA size implication using our technique.
However, we added data with structure specific ssDNA nucleases. Both ExoT (3’-5’ssDNA exonuclease) and RecJ (5-3’ssDNA exonuclease), which cannot act on dsDNA, degrade the RF structures detected by ssDNA-SIRF. This shows that both 3’ and 5’ ssDNA exists at these sites (added Fig 3e and Ext Data Figs.3h,i)
4. Could the authors perform a time-course experiment to assess whether RF-SIRF signals increase during genotoxic treatment in the presence of nuclease inhibitors such as Mirin?
To further address how reversed forks form, we added a time course experiment for RF-SIRF. This validates the idea that it is predominantly the nascent DNA prior to DNA damage that forms RF-SIRF signals (Ext. Data Fig. 1h-j)
MRE11 in the context of fork reversal formation is currently being actively investigated by several group. Inhibition with mirin would be insufficient to address any role for MRE11 during fork reversal, and this merits a separate full study that goes beyond the scope of this manuscript. Moreover, time course experiments with MRE11 are likely to heavily change the EdU concentrations, which will render interpretations difficult. We added discussion about the challenge in interpretation and the importance in considering total amounts of EdU to the discussion.
.
5. The authors present convincing evidence that ssDNA can be detected at reversed forks upon resection. It would be valuable to demonstrate that the RF-SIRF signal decreases as ssDNA-SIRF increases. A time-course experiment in BRCA2-deficient cells could illustrate these signal dynamics.
To our knowledge, there is no evidence for reversed forks containing blunt ends. Rather by the nature of their formation, reversed forks contain ssDNA overhangs at least initially, which are either 3’ or 5’ depending on if the leading or lagging strand are ahead.
To this end, we have added data demonstrating this using structure specific ssDNA nucleases. Both ExoT (3’-5’ssDNA exonuclease) and RecJ (5-3’ssDNA exonuclease), which cannot act on dsDNA, degrade the RF structures detected by ssDNA-SIRF, showing that both 3’ and 5’ ssDNA exists at these sites (Fig 3e and Ext. Data Fig. 3g,h).
While we believe that RF-SIRF is a key advance in studying fork reversal and reversed forks, like any technique, it has its limitations. In this case, the signals are directly dependent on the total EdU molarity in addition to proximity. Both nascent DNA degradation (as expected in BRCA2 defective cells) and residual incorporation during extended periods of time (e.g. see added Ext. Data. Fig 1d, showing continued residual incorporation of EdU) can cause changes in EdU moieties. This multi-valent EdU changes make any RF-SIRF interpretation for a time course experiments in BRCA2 deficient cells speculative. We now better discuss RF-SIRF limitations in the discussion.
6. The EdU-H3K9me and H4K16ac-EdU PLA experiments do not presently add substantial value, as the authors do not directly demonstrate that the observed signal arises from reversed forks. Unless supported by further experimental validation, this section should be removed.
We have added multiple data figures (Fig. 7 and Ext. Data Fig. 7) to better demonstrate and clarify the advances and discoveries. Our initial data showed that both H3K9me3 (classically transcription repressing) and H3K4me3 (classically transcription activating) increase with fork reversal (e.g. decrease with SMARCAL1 knockdown). From a simple transcriptional epigenetic point of view, these results appear contradicting. However, we now furthermore show that H3K9me3 and H3K4me3 are co-occurring upon for reversal (Fig. 7a,b): this suggests distinct specificity for these otherwise rare bi-valent epigenetic marks at reversed forks. Thus, these data corroborate our interpretation of a replication specific epigenetic language that is distinct from the transcriptional epigenetic code.
Total H3-SIRF on the other hand slightly decreases rather than increases at reversed forks, suggesting active epigenetic changes at stalled forks (Fig. 7c,d and Ext. Data Fig. 7b,c). Consistently, we find that these epigenetic marks at reversed forks are dependent on PTIP, which is a MLL3/4-binding partner required for H3K4 tri-methylation, validating the epigenetic changes at stalled and reversed forks as new events (Fig. 7e,f and Ext. Data Fig. 7d,e)
The advance in this data is that our results highlight replication-stress specific epigenetic changes that previously were not appreciated despite the clear understanding that single specific epigenetic marks recruit or repress distinct DDR proteins. Our data establish specific epigenetic marks or codes at stressed and reversed replication forks. Despite the fact that they are classically incompatible from a transcriptional view angle, these findings can explain how replication stress response proteins are recruited to stalled forks in the face of opposing epigenetic changes from a transcriptional view point.
